doc.title: Dan Barrett interviewed by Michael Woods, Los Angeles, California, September 3, 1995

title: Goodman's rehearsal test with no rhythm section
summary: Goodman demands both perfection and swing; he sends the rhythm section out and makes the horns keep time silently until they land the bridge together.

story.theme_name: Working for Benny Goodman: the leader and his bands
story.community_name: Working for Benny Goodman: the perfectionist bandleader

blocks.x: Describe that for us. Kind of give us a hypothetical.

Well his standards were so high. In fact one trumpet player at the trumpet player’s first rehearsal, I think I’d made two or three rehearsals, this trumpet player came in and we finished the rehearsal and ran to the nearest bar I think, the whole band, en masse. The trumpet player was shaking his head and I said, “John, what’s wrong?” He said, “I can’t figure this guy out.” I said, “who, Goodman?” He said, “yeah.” I said, “well what can’t you figure out?” And he said, “well he wants everything to swing, but he wants it perfect, but he wants it to swing, but he wants it perfect.” And I said, “yeah.” And he said, “well I’m used to like laid back band leaders. They don’t care about everything being precise as long as it swings.” And he says, “I’ve worked for other band leaders, they don’t want to know about swinging, they want every note perfectly in place.” He said, “this guy wants both.” And I said, “yeah, that’s why he’s Benny Goodman.” And he didn’t ask us to do anything that he wasn’t doing himself. I mean he worked the hardest at his age. He was in his middle 70s then and he’d, he was famous for this, and it was true, I’d read about this and then finally he did it with us. He would have the whole band there, and then he’d tell the rhythm section to get lost for 45 minutes. He’d say, “go off and get some coffee and come back in 45 minutes or an hour. Take an hour off.” And the guys in the rhythm section shrugged their shoulders and take off, so that left the saxophone section and the trumpets and trombones. And he’d say, “okay, start it at the top, one, two, one two three.” And the first time we did this, we came in and the rhythm fell back, almost imperceptibly. But he waved us off and he said, “no, that isn’t where I kicked it off. Now do it again.” And it was a little frightening, a little intimidating you know? “One, two, one two three” and we came in again and we got through about 16 bars then before it — hey Wendell — before it settled down a little bit. And he waved us off again you know. And he said, “I’m not going to play with a band that can’t keep time. Now do it again, and this time keep time.” You know, “okay.” And he kicked it off again, and we got through the first chorus, and he said, “keep going.” Now this is with no rhythm section you know. And there were places where the piano would normally play fills, well those were just big open spaces. And he said, “no foot tapping — I don’t want to hear anybody count — count in your mind.” And we kept going and then finally there was a bridge. And we were all frightened to death but we were keeping it going, and there was a bridge where it was a piano solo with the rhythm section for eight bars. And we’re all counting

eight bars like this silently, and then we came in [snaps fingers] about like that, I mean almost exactly but not quite, and we thought he was going to bite our heads off and he started laughing. He thought that was pretty funny. Because he knew how difficult that was.
